evidence.claim: ATI Industrial Automation (acquired by Novanta) is the global standard for 6-axis force/torque sensors in robotics; virtually every research humanoid and early commercial deployment uses ATI sensors (Mini45, Axia series); market share estimated at 60-70% of precision F/T sensor market
evidence.source: ATI product dominance in academic robotics literature; supply chain analysis; humanoid OEM BOM reviews

evidence.claim: ATI F/T sensors cost $3,000-$8,000 each; a humanoid with 4 sensors (both wrists, both ankles) incurs $12,000-$32,000 in F/T sensor costs — 10-25% of robot BOM at current pricing; no alternative achieves equivalent precision at lower cost as of 2025
evidence.source: ATI product pricing; humanoid BOM analysis; industry cost breakdowns

evidence.claim: Novanta acquired ATI in 2021; Novanta is a precision technology company (Nasdaq: NOVT) with ~$850M revenue; medical devices and robotics are primary segments; humanoid robot demand is a new significant growth vector not yet in consensus analyst models
evidence.source: Novanta investor materials; ATI acquisition announcement; Novanta annual reports

evidence.claim: F/T sensor calibration and signal processing IP is as important as the mechanical structure; ATI's proprietary calibration algorithms and temperature compensation are barriers to substitution beyond just the physical sensor design
evidence.source: ATI technical documentation; robotics application engineering analysis

what_could_weaken_view: Low-cost F/T alternatives emerge at scale: Bota Systems (Switzerland), Sunrise Instruments (China), and internal solutions from humanoid OEMs are all targeting $500-$1,500 per sensor — if any achieves ATI-equivalent precision, the pricing umbrella collapses
Humanoid OEMs develop proprietary F/T sensing: Tesla and Figure AI both have large hardware teams; in-house F/T sensor development would eliminate ATI dependency for the largest volume customers
ATI is a minority of Novanta revenue: Novanta's medical device and laser motion control segments are larger; the stock is not a pure-play on humanoid F/T sensing, diluting the financial leverage

Tactile sensing replaces discrete F/T sensors: distributed tactile sensor arrays on robot hands/feet could provide equivalent force information without discrete 6-axis sensors at each wrist/ankle — reduces addressable market
